anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys and downstream consumers fall behind because they cannot receive or apply WAL/redo traffic as fast as the primary generates it.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network paths, listeners, or session slots saturate or flap, delaying or aborting client and replica connections as well as log streaming.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database exhibits a multi-layered slowdown: tables and indexes bloat, full-table scans and index probes lengthen, and primary commit latency rises as replication send queues back up. Replication lag metrics climb while replica read staleness grows; simultaneously, clients and replication workers suffer connection timeouts, increased round-trip times, and frequent reconnect storms that exhaust server connection slots. Log-segment retention balloons because lagging replicas and disconnected receivers prevent recycling, which in turn increases disk-space pressure and prolongs crash-recovery and backup windows. Planner misestimates due to MVCC bloat further amplify load on the primary, and the resulting higher write throughput aggravates both network saturation and replica replay deficits.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn creates rapid version buildup, enlarging the write-ahead log volume that must be shipped over the network. The swollen WAL stream competes with application traffic on constrained or unstable network links, elevating packet loss and retransmissions and causing receiver backends to stall or drop. Each disconnect forces replication to restart log streaming, multiplying network handshakes and further delaying apply. The sustained replica lag holds old transaction snapshots open, slowing vacuum/cleaner progress and locking in even more dead rows on the primary, which inflates table size and write rates—a feedback loop that perpetuates version bloat, network congestion, and replication backlog until storage or connection capacity is exhausted.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
